1. INTRODUCTION
Since their discovery in 2007 (Lorimer et al. 2007), the
nature of the progenitor(s) of fast radio bursts (FRBs) has
been of great interest.
Enabled by precise radio localisa-
tions of FRBs (Chatterjee et al. 2017; Bannister et al. 2019),
various authors have analysed increasingly large samples
of FRB host galaxies (Bhandari et al. 2020; Li & Zhang
2020; Heintz et al. 2020; Bhandari et al. 2022; Gordon et al.
2023). Their results have yielded broadly consistent conclu-
sions with increasing precision: that the host galaxies of ap-
parently once-off FRBs are inconsistent with the high-star-
formation rate dwarf galaxies expected from superluminous
supernovae (SLSNe) and long-duration gamma-ray bursts
(LGRBs) (Fruchter et al. 2006), while repeating FRBs tend
to be found in such galaxies (Tendulkar et al. 2017); FRBs
rarely occur in “red and dead” galaxies which have ceased
star-formation (e.g. Shah et al. 2025; Eftekhari et al. 2025),
and do not trace total stellar mass (e.g. Safarzadeh et al.
2020); their mass-metallicity follows standard 0.07 < z <
0.7 relations (Heintz et al. 2020); and their host populations
are broadly consistent with those of core-collapse supernovae
(CCSNe) and short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs).
Most recently, Sharma et al. (2024) expanded the sample
with 30 host galaxies detected by the Deep Synoptic Ar-
ray (DSA), confirming both the trend of FRBs tracing star-
formation in high-mass galaxies, and a possible deficit of

low-mass host galaxies compared to expectations from star-
formation in the FRB host sample. In particular, the authors
identify a break point of approximately 1010 M∗[M⊙], above
which FRB hosts do trace star formation, and they argue this
is evidence for FRBs being associated with high metallicity
environments.
In this work, we consider the degree to which the FRB’s lo-
calisation causes a bias in identifying the FRB host galaxy in
optical images from radio localisations, and hence, whether
or not the observed deficit of dwarf hosts may be explained
by such a bias.
2. A BIAS IN FRB HOST GALAXIES?
Fast radio burst host galaxies are identified from optical
follow-up observations in the direction of the radio signal,
with an optical counterpart coincident with the radio locali-
sation region being taken as evidence for that galaxy being
the true host.
This process produces a bias against low-
luminosity FRB host galaxies in two ways.
Firstly, such
galaxies will in-general be dimmer, and hence less likely to
be detected in optical images. Secondly, the prevalence of
low-luminsoity galaxies makes the firm identification of any
given one as the true host more difficult, even if it is detected
in the image. The importance of very precise radio localisa-
tion in identifying low-luminosity FRB hosts was highlighted
by Eftekhari & Berger (2017), who noted that a localisation
accuracy of 0.5” would be required to identify a dwarf FRB
host galaxy at z ≥0.1 at 99% confidence. Hence, dwarf
FRB hosts will be less likely to be confidently identified, and

in a manner which is dependent upon the radio localisation
accuracy.
The current standard method for quantifying the level of
confidence in FRB host galaxy identification is the Probabal-
istic Association of Transients to their Hosts (PATH; Aggar-
wal et al. 2021). This Bayesian method applies a Jeffrey’s
prior P(O) according to a galaxy’s magnitude (typically the
r-band magnitude, mr); a prior P(θ/ϕ) on the distribution of
angular offsets θ of an FRB from the host centre relative to
its half-light radius ϕ; and the probability P(U) of the true
host being unseen in the image. PATH also accounts for the
radio localisation precision, usually in the form of an ellip-
tical Gaussian. The output is a posterior estimate, P(O|x),
of each host galaxy candidate’s probability of being the true
host, and a probability P(U|x) of the true host remaining
undetected.
A full determination of any possible bias in PATH would
be complex, and depend on the assumed underlying distribu-
tion of FRB host galaxies. Here, we perform a simple test of
this potential bias using FRBs detected by the CRAFT Inco-
herent Sum (‘ICS’) survey (Shannon et al. 2024).
3. SIMULATION OF THE BIAS USING THE
ASKAP/CRAFT ICS SAMPLE
The ASKAP ICS survey recently reported the detection of
43 FRBs (Shannon et al. 2024). Of these, 37 had interfero-
metric localisations with typical accuracy of 0.5”. A PATH
analysis identified 30 host galaxies at > 95% confidence.
We study the effect of localisation accuracy on this host
galaxy sample by artificially degrading the localisation ac-
curacy, and re-running the PATH analysis using the 32 host
galaxies with deep imaging (i.e. complete to an r-band mag-
nitude of at least 25) currently provided in the FRB reposi-
tory (Prochaska et al. 2019) with tables of PATH outputs. To
do so, we increase the true localisation uncertainty, σtrue, to
a certain minimum, σmin, to generate a new localisation un-

the resulting host magnitude distribution. For this analysis,
we use a prior on the probability of the true host being un-
seen, P(U), of 0.1, comparable to that used in the work of
Sharma et al. (2024).
Figure 1 shows the cumulative distribution of firm host
galaxy magnitudes for σmin = 0.5′′ −10′′.
We find no
effect for σmin = 1′′ and below, but that for σmin = 2′′
and above, the probability of identifying a low-luminosity
(mr > 21.5) host decreases, and the cumulative distribution
of host magnitudes shifts downwards, to brighter galaxies.
For σmin = 5′′, very high-magnitude galaxies (mr < 19) are
favoured above those in the (19 < mr < 21) range. When
σmin = 10′′, no host galaxy is confidently identified.
4. CONCLUSION
We have tested the predictions of Eftekhari & Berger
(2017) regarding the required accuracy to confidently iden-
tify FRB host galaxies, using a real sample of localised FRBs
detected by ASKAP/CRAFT, and the PATH statistical frame-
work. We have shown that increased uncertainty in localisa-
tion accuracy begins to affect the implied FRB host galaxy
magnitude distribution in the ASKAP ICS survey for local-
isation precisions ≥2
′′. We do not therefore expect there
to be a significant localisation bias in the ASKAP and DSA
FRB samples — which have typical localistion accuracies
of ≤1′′ — that are used in an analysis of FRB host galax-
ies. MeerTRAP coherent FRB detection data should be like-
wise useful (Jankowski et al. 2023). Note that this is not a
comprehensive review of potential sources of bias in such
analyses, and we do not exclude that other sources of bias
may be present. For instance, the localisation accuracy of
CHIME FRBs prior to the use of outriggers is several ar-
cminutes (CHIME/FRB Collaboration: Amiri et al. 2021),
and several FRBs detected by CHIME were used in the anal-
ysis of Sharma et al. (2024).

**Structured Highlights for the Research Paper:**

---

### **1. Core Innovation**
The research introduces a systematic evaluation of the impact of radio localisation precision on the identification of fast radio burst (FRB) host galaxies. Using the ASKAP ICS survey as a foundation, the study employs the Probabalistic Association of Transients to their Hosts (PATH) algorithm to analyze how varying levels of radio localisation uncertainty affect the reliability of host galaxy detection, particularly for low-luminosity galaxies.

---

### **2. Technical Approach**
- **Simulated Localisation Errors**: The study artificially increases radio localisation uncertainty from 0.5" to 10" to assess its effect on the PATH algorithm's performance.
- **PATH Algorithm**: Utilizes a Bayesian framework with priors on galaxy magnitude (mr), angular offset distribution, and the probability of the true host being undetected.
- **Cumulative Distribution Analysis**: Compares the cumulative distribution of host galaxy magnitudes for different levels of localisation uncertainty, revealing shifts in the probability of confidently identifying low-luminosity galaxies.

---

### **3. Quantitative Findings**
1. **Minimal Uncertainty (0.5"–1"):** No significant bias is observed in host galaxy identification.
2. **Moderate Uncertainty (2"–5"):** A noticeable shift towards brighter galaxies is observed, with a decrease in the probability of identifying low-luminosity galaxies.
3. **High Uncertainty (5"–10"):** The cumulative distribution of host magnitudes shifts further, with very high-magnitude galaxies dominating, and no confident identification of low-luminosity galaxies for 10" uncertainty.

---

### **4. Limitations & Assumptions**
- **Assumption of Host Galaxy Distribution**: The analysis assumes a standard distribution of FRB host galaxies, potentially limiting applicability to diverse environments.
- **Magnitude Thresholds**: The study focuses on hosts with r-band magnitudes above 25, excluding lower luminosity galaxies.
- **Localisation Errors**: The simulation assumes uniform application of localisation uncertainty across all sources, which may not reflect real-world variations.

---

### **5. Domain Impact**
- **Theoretical**: Highlights the critical role of radio localisation precision in FRB host galaxy identification, providing a framework for understanding observational biases.
- **Practical**: The findings are crucial for interpreting FRB data, particularly in distinguishing between high and low-luminosity host galaxies, and inform the design of future surveys to mitigate biases.

---

### **Key Equations/Figures**
- **Localisation Error Impact**: The cumulative distribution of host magnitudes shifts with increasing localisation uncertainty, as shown in **Figure 1**.
- **PATH Algorithm Probability**: The posterior probability P(O|x) and the probability of the true host being undetected P(U|x) are central to the Bayesian framework.

---

This structured approach provides a clear understanding of the research's methodology, findings, and implications for the field of radio astronomy and FRB host galaxy studies.
